content.title: Adult Essential Hypertension Screening and Confirmation

pathophysiology.summary: Essential hypertension is persistently elevated arterial blood pressure without an identified secondary cause. It is often asymptomatic and increases cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and kidney risk.
keyMechanisms: Interactions among genetic, renal, vascular, neurohormonal, and environmental factors
Increased systemic vascular resistance and altered sodium-volume regulation
Cumulative pressure-related vascular and target-organ injury

symptoms: Usually asymptomatic
Occasional non-specific headache or dizziness, which cannot establish diagnosis
physicalSigns: Elevated pressure on correctly performed measurement
Possible target-organ disease in established hypertension
Possible clinical clues to a secondary cause
redFlags: Severe elevation with chest pain, dyspnoea, neurological deficit, confusion, visual loss, or acute kidney injury
Pregnancy with elevated pressure or pre-eclampsia symptoms
Abrupt onset, resistant readings, or suspected secondary cause

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Clinic readings elevated but validated out-of-office average not persistently elevated.
Clinic readings may be below threshold while home or ambulatory readings are elevated.
Young onset, abrupt worsening, resistance, relevant medicines, renal or endocrine clues.
Pain, anxiety, acute illness, stimulants, or measurement error; repeat under standardised conditions.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Repeated standardised clinic blood-pressure measurement — Persistent elevated blood pressure
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Repeat valid readings and compare with the current Saudi diagnostic threshold.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Avoids diagnosis from an isolated or technically inaccurate reading.

references.title: Saudi MOH: Cardiometabolic Risk Management — Assessment of Hypertension
references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Home or ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring — Sustained, white-coat or masked hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Compare out-of-office averages with clinic readings using the appropriate thresholds.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms the blood-pressure pattern before long-term management decisions.

references.title: Saudi MOH: Cardiometabolic Risk Management — Assessment of Hypertension
references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serum creatinine and eGFR — Reduced kidney filtration
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Raised creatinine or reduced eGFR warrants assessment against prior results.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Detects renal involvement and provides a treatment-safety baseline.

references.title: Saudi MOH: Cardiometabolic Risk Management — Assessment of Hypertension
references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serum potassium and sodium — Electrolyte disturbance
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Low potassium may suggest a secondary cause or medicine effect.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identifies secondary-cause clues and informs safe medicine selection.

references.title: Saudi MOH: Cardiometabolic Risk Management — Assessment of Hypertension
references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Urine albumin-creatinine ratio — Renal albumin leakage
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Raised albumin excretion suggests kidney damage; confirm as appropriate.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Identifies renal target-organ involvement and modifies risk assessment.

references.title: Saudi MOH: Cardiometabolic Risk Management — Assessment of Hypertension
references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Urinalysis — Haematuria, protein or abnormal urinary sediment
ruleIn.targetCondition: Haematuria, protein or abnormal urinary sediment
ruleIn.expectedFinding: An abnormal result directs renal evaluation.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Looks for kidney disease as a cause or consequence of hypertension.

references.title: Saudi MOH: Cardiometabolic Risk Management — Assessment of Hypertension
references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: 12-lead electrocardiogram — Left-ventricular hypertrophy, ischaemic change or arrhythmia
ruleIn.targetCondition: Left-ventricular hypertrophy, ischaemic change or arrhythmia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Relevant ECG changes identify cardiac involvement; a normal ECG does not exclude it.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assesses cardiac consequences and competing cardiovascular disease.

references.edition: Legacy manual, PDF pages 35–36; check current local pathway

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Lipid profile and glycaemia assessment — Dyslipidaemia or diabetes accompanying hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Abnormal lipid/glucose results change cardiovascular-risk assessment.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines coexisting modifiable risk factors.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Aldosterone-renin testing when primary aldosteronism is suspected — Inappropriate aldosterone activity
ruleOut.targetCondition: Inappropriate aldosterone activity
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Interpret the ratio with potassium, medicines and sampling conditions.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Investigates resistant hypertension or relevant hypokalaemia under a specialist/local pathway.

ruleOut.targetCondition: Catecholamine excess
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Raised results need contextual interpretation and confirmatory assessment.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Investigates suggestive episodic symptoms or other relevant clinical clues.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Sleep study when obstructive sleep apnoea is suspected — Sleep-related obstructive breathing events

ruleOut.expectedFinding: A diagnostic study establishes clinically important sleep-disordered breathing.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Tests a suspected contributor; it is not routine for every hypertensive patient.

clinicalManagement.title: Screen and measure accurately
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Preventive and primary-care encounters, or when indicated
actions: Use a validated device, correct cuff, and standardised seated measurement after rest.
Obtain repeat readings and document method, values, symptoms, and context.
Review medicines, supplements, stimulants, tobacco, pain, and acute illness.
Do not diagnose from one isolated value unless urgent circumstances require action.

branches.condition: Elevated screening measurement without acute symptoms
actions: Arrange repeat and out-of-office confirmation within a risk-appropriate interval.
Explain follow-up and symptoms needing urgent assessment.

branches.condition: Severe elevation with possible acute target-organ injury
actions: Arrange immediate emergency assessment.
Avoid rapid unsupervised outpatient lowering.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm diagnosis and assess risk
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After elevated screening readings
actions: Confirm sustained hypertension with repeated clinic and/or validated out-of-office readings.
Assess cardiovascular risk, kidney function, diabetes, lipids, smoking, and target-organ injury.
Investigate secondary causes when clinical indications are present.
Agree an individualised plan and follow-up interval.

branches.condition: Out-of-office values are not persistently elevated
actions: Consider white-coat hypertension rather than labelling sustained disease.
Continue monitoring based on overall risk.

branches.condition: Secondary cause or target-organ injury suspected
actions: Arrange targeted work-up and specialist input as appropriate.
Address urgent complications through emergency care.

clinicalManagement.title: Reduce risk and provide ongoing care
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After diagnosis and at regular follow-up
actions: Offer lifestyle measures and treatment options under current local guidance.
Select medication when indicated based on comorbidities, renal function, pregnancy potential, contraindications, and preference.
Review pressure, adherence, adverse effects, renal function, and risk after treatment changes.
Escalate persistent uncontrolled readings or suspected complications.

branches.condition: Pregnancy or pregnancy potential
actions: Use a pregnancy-specific assessment and treatment pathway.
Review medicines promptly and involve obstetric care when indicated.

branches.condition: Pressure remains above agreed target
actions: Confirm measurement technique and adherence; review interfering medicines and secondary causes.
Adjust treatment or refer under local guidance.

patientEducation: Explain that hypertension is often symptom-free and needs accurate measurement and follow-up.
Teach home-monitoring technique when used.
Explain urgent symptoms requiring immediate assessment.
lifestyleAndDiet: Discuss balanced eating and sodium reduction where appropriate.
Encourage regular activity, healthy weight goals, and tobacco cessation.
Discuss alcohol use consistent with health needs and local advice.
mdtReferrals: Primary care or family medicine
Dietitian or lifestyle support
Cardiology, nephrology, or endocrinology when indicated
Obstetrics for pregnancy-associated hypertension
dischargeCriteria: Measurement result, confirmation plan, and precautions are documented.
Acute target-organ injury is assessed and disposition determined.
Patient knows when blood pressure will be reassessed.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange repeat clinic or out-of-office measurements and cardiovascular-risk review according to results, patient risk, and local guidance.

pathophysiology.summary: A mechanical blockage or dysmotility causes proximal dilation and fluid sequestration. A closed-loop obstruction can compromise venous and arterial supply, leading to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: A mechanical blockage or dysmotility causes proximal dilation and fluid sequestration. A closed-loop obstruction can compromise venous and arterial supply, leading to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Acute Bowel Obstruction, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.
redFlags: Continuous severe pain or peritonism
Shock, fever with toxicity, or metabolic acidosis
Strangulated hernia
Free air or suspected bowel ischaemia

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Diffuse bowel dilation without a mechanical transition; consider medicines and recent illness/surgery.
Diarrhoea and absence of progressive distension may support an alternative.
Pain out of proportion or peritonism requires emergency action.

ruleIn.testName: CT abdomen/pelvis when indicated by the surgical team
ruleIn.modalityTarget: CT abdomen/pelvis when indicated by the surgical team — Obstruction level, transition point, closed loop or bowel compromise
ruleIn.targetCondition: Obstruction level, transition point, closed loop or bowel compromise
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Dilated bowel with a transition point; reduced enhancement, free fluid or perforation features raise concern for compromised bowel.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines anatomy and complications that change the urgency and type of surgical intervention.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Serum electrolytes and creatinine — Dehydration, kidney injury and electrolyte losses
ruleIn.targetCondition: Dehydration, kidney injury and electrolyte losses
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Potassium or sodium disturbance and rising creatinine after vomiting or reduced intake.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides a baseline for fluid replacement and correction of electrolyte losses.

ruleOut.testName: Lactate and blood gas when ischaemia or shock is suspected
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Lactate and blood gas when ischaemia or shock is suspected — Hypoperfusion and metabolic acidosis
ruleOut.targetCondition: Hypoperfusion and metabolic acidosis
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Raised lactate or acidosis increases concern; normal early results do not exclude bowel ischaemia.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Supports urgent reassessment alongside examination and imaging; it cannot safely exclude strangulation alone.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess urgency, stability, and the person’s priorities
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At first contact and whenever the situation changes
actions: Confirm the presenting concern, relevant timeline, baseline function, medicines, allergies, comorbidities, and the patient’s immediate priorities.
Assess the red flags above and use the current local escalation pathway if instability or rapid deterioration is present.
Explain uncertainty and involve the patient or appropriate decision-maker in a way suited to the setting.

branches.condition: A red flag, instability, or rapid deterioration is present
actions: Escalate immediately to the responsible senior or emergency team using the local pathway.
Stabilise and investigate in parallel; do not delay time-critical action for routine testing.

branches.condition: The person is stable for a planned or longitudinal pathway
actions: Proceed with focused assessment and shared planning.
Document the threshold for urgent reassessment.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm the working diagnosis and stratify risk
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly; adapt timing to acuity
actions: Use the history, examination, and investigations listed above to confirm the likely process and assess important alternatives.
Interpret results using current national/local diagnostic criteria, age, pregnancy status, comorbidity, and prior results.
Record severity, uncertainty, and which findings would change the plan.

branches.condition: The diagnosis remains uncertain or tests conflict with the clinical picture
actions: Reassess the history and examination and seek senior or specialty advice.
Use targeted additional testing only when its result can change management.

branches.condition: A high-risk complication or an alternative diagnosis is identified
actions: Switch to the relevant urgent or specialty pathway.
Communicate the finding and handover responsibility clearly.

clinicalManagement.title: Agree evidence-informed care and address the cause
clinicalManagement.timeframe: According to acuity and current local protocol
actions: Use the topic-specific focus in this record to agree immediate and longer-term priorities with the patient.
Select treatment only after checking current local guidance, formulary, contraindications, interactions, organ function, pregnancy considerations, and patient preference.
Treat reversible contributors and address access, communication, cultural, and functional barriers.

branches.condition: Treatment is ineffective, poorly tolerated, or inconsistent with the patient’s goals
actions: Reassess diagnosis, treatment burden, adherence barriers, and alternatives with the responsible specialist.
Document the shared decision and safety-net plan.

branches.condition: The patient improves on the agreed plan
actions: Continue the plan with monitoring proportional to risk.
Provide clear instructions for expected course and warning symptoms.

clinicalManagement.title: Coordinate handover, education, and follow-up
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before transition and at the agreed review interval
actions: Provide a written plan stating the working diagnosis, key findings, medicines or interventions, monitoring, and who owns each next step.
Use teach-back to check that the patient or caregiver understands warning symptoms, follow-up, and how to obtain help.
Close the loop on pending results, referrals, and screening or prevention actions.

branches.condition: Safe care cannot be delivered in the current setting
actions: Arrange a higher level of care or supported transfer and send a structured clinical handover.
Confirm transport, caregiver, and communication needs where relevant.

branches.condition: The patient is ready for outpatient or continuing care
actions: Confirm a feasible follow-up date and contact route.
Document when and how the plan should be reviewed or escalated.

patientEducation: Explain acute bowel obstruction in plain language, including what is known, what remains uncertain, and how the plan will be reviewed.
Use teach-back for warning signs, medicines or monitoring, and the route to urgent help.
Invite questions and adapt written or interpreted information to the patient’s language, health literacy, and communication needs.
lifestyleAndDiet: Offer topic-relevant prevention or self-management support that is safe, feasible, culturally appropriate, and consistent with the person’s goals.
Avoid one-size-fits-all restrictions; individualise advice for pregnancy, frailty, kidney/heart disease, disability, and treatment burden.
mdtReferrals: Acute Care Surgery / Emergency Medicine
Primary care or the responsible continuity team
Pharmacist, nurse educator, dietitian, rehabilitation, mental-health, or social support when relevant to the case.
dischargeCriteria: Clinical status is appropriate for the next setting, and urgent complications have been excluded or addressed.
The patient or caregiver has an understandable plan, access to needed treatment/support, and a clear escalation route.
Pending investigations and referrals have a named owner and follow-up timeframe.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review the topic-specific focus, patient goals, symptoms and function at an interval matched to risk. Reconcile new results and treatment effects, close referrals, and revisit the plan if the condition, circumstances, or preferences change.

pathophysiology.summary: Airway inflammation and mucus increase expiratory flow limitation and dynamic hyperinflation; infection or pollutants can worsen ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Severe episodes may cause hypercapnia, fatigue, and respiratory muscle failure. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Airway inflammation and mucus increase expiratory flow limitation and dynamic hyperinflation
infection or pollutants can worsen ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Severe episodes may cause hypercapnia, fatigue, and respiratory muscle failure.

symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Acute Exacerbation of COPD, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.
redFlags: Severe hypoxaemia or rising carbon dioxide with acidosis
Exhaustion, confusion, or silent chest
Haemodynamic instability
Sudden pleuritic pain or unilateral reduced breath sounds

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fever, focal findings, or infiltrate may indicate concurrent infection.
Congestion may coexist and change fluid or respiratory decisions.
Consider when onset, pain, hypoxaemia, or examination is disproportionate.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Pulse oximetry — Hypoxaemia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced oxygen saturation; oximetry does not measure carbon dioxide or exclude hypercapnia.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Guides titrated oxygen and identifies the need for blood-gas assessment.

ruleIn.testName: Arterial blood gas when respiratory failure is suspected
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Arterial blood gas when respiratory failure is suspected — Hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Raised carbon dioxide with reduced pH indicates ventilatory failure; compare with prior results and repeat when clinically indicated.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Helps determine ventilatory support and monitor response to treatment.

ruleOut.testName: Chest radiograph when clinically indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Chest radiograph when clinically indicated — Pneumonia, pneumothorax or pulmonary oedema
ruleOut.targetCondition: Pneumonia, pneumothorax or pulmonary oedema
ruleOut.expectedFinding: New focal opacity, pleural air or congestion suggests a cause beyond an uncomplicated exacerbation.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies treatable mimics and complications that require a different pathway.

ruleOut.testName: 12-lead ECG when cardiac disease is suspected
ruleOut.modalityTarget: 12-lead ECG when cardiac disease is suspected — Ischaemia or arrhythmia
ruleOut.targetCondition: Ischaemia or arrhythmia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: New ischaemic changes or a significant rhythm disturbance; a normal ECG does not exclude coronary disease.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Cardiac disease may precipitate or mimic respiratory deterioration.

content.title: Acute Heart Failure and Pulmonary Oedema

pathophysiology.summary: Raised filling pressures cause pulmonary or systemic venous congestion; impaired output and neurohormonal activation can worsen renal sodium retention. Acute triggers may include ischaemia, arrhythmia, infection, uncontrolled blood pressure, medication interruption, or renal deterioration. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Raised filling pressures cause pulmonary or systemic venous congestion

impaired output and neurohormonal activation can worsen renal sodium retention. Acute triggers may include ischaemia, arrhythmia, infection, uncontrolled blood pressure, medication interruption, or renal deterioration.

symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Acute Heart Failure and Pulmonary Oedema, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.
redFlags: Severe hypoxaemia or exhaustion
Hypotension, cool peripheries, or shock
Ongoing ischaemic chest pain or dangerous arrhythmia
Altered consciousness or rapidly worsening respiratory distress

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fever or focal findings may coexist with congestion.
Acute pleuritic symptoms and thromboembolic risk require structured assessment.
Wheeze does not exclude simultaneous cardiac congestion.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Chest radiograph — Pulmonary congestion and pleural effusions
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Interstitial or alveolar oedema and effusions may be present; absence does not exclude early heart failure.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Assesses congestion and alternative thoracic causes of acute dyspnoea.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Echocardiography — Ventricular dysfunction or an acute structural cause
ruleIn.targetCondition: Ventricular dysfunction or an acute structural cause
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced ventricular function, important valve disease or other structural abnormality; preserved ejection fraction does not exclude heart failure.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines the cardiac phenotype and detects causes needing urgent specialist intervention.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Creatinine and electrolytes — Kidney dysfunction and sodium/potassium disturbance
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Renal impairment or electrolyte abnormality at baseline or during treatment.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Informs safe diuresis, medication selection and monitoring.

ruleOut.testName: 12-lead ECG and troponin when ACS is suspected
ruleOut.modalityTarget: 12-lead ECG and troponin when ACS is suspected — Acute coronary ischaemia or a significant arrhythmia
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute coronary ischaemia or a significant arrhythmia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Ischaemic ECG changes or a troponin rise/fall require interpretation with symptoms; troponin may rise in heart failure without ACS.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies a precipitant requiring a parallel cardiac emergency pathway.

pathophysiology.summary: Reduced renal perfusion, parenchymal injury, or urinary obstruction can lower filtration; these mechanisms may coexist. Sepsis, medicines, glomerular disease, and fluid depletion can lead to electrolyte, acid-base, and volume complications. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Reduced renal perfusion, parenchymal injury, or urinary obstruction can lower filtration
these mechanisms may coexist. Sepsis, medicines, glomerular disease, and fluid depletion can lead to electrolyte, acid-base, and volume complications.

content.title: Delirium and Agitation Near End of Life

pathophysiology.summary: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness caused by interacting vulnerability and precipitating factors. Near end of life, illness, medicines, dehydration, pain, retention, and environment may contribute. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness caused by interacting vulnerability and precipitating factors. Near end of life, illness, medicines, dehydration, pain, retention, and environment may contribute.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

Respiratory compromise or suspected toxicity
Unsafe agitation or risk of injury
Family distress with unresolved goals or uncertainty

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Acute fluctuation and inattention suggest delirium over baseline decline.

differentials.condition: Medication toxicity, infection, retention, constipation, dehydration
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Common reversible contributors to assess.

ruleIn.testName: Collateral history and validated delirium assessment
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Collateral history and validated delirium assessment — Acute fluctuating inattention or cognitive change
ruleIn.targetCondition: Acute fluctuating inattention or cognitive change
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A change from baseline with fluctuation and impaired attention supports delirium.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Distinguishes delirium from chronic cognitive impairment and establishes the time course.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Pain, bladder, bowel and medication assessment — Reversible causes of distress
ruleOut.targetCondition: Reversible causes of distress
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Pain, retention, constipation or a recent deliriogenic medicine may explain agitation.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Detects treatable contributors without automatically adding invasive investigations.

ruleOut.testName: Targeted glucose, electrolytes or infection tests when goal-concordant
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Targeted glucose, electrolytes or infection tests when goal-concordant — A suspected metabolic or infectious precipitant
ruleOut.targetCondition: A suspected metabolic or infectious precipitant
ruleOut.expectedFinding: An abnormal result is interpreted against the suspected cause and goals of care.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Order only the named tests likely to change symptom-focused treatment.

ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Reduces misclassification from biological variation, acute illness or testing error.

pathophysiology.summary: Insulin deficiency and counter-regulatory hormones increase lipolysis and hepatic ketone production; osmotic diuresis produces water and electrolyte loss. Infection, interrupted insulin, new diabetes, medicines, or acute stress may precipitate crisis. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

osmotic diuresis produces water and electrolyte loss. Infection, interrupted insulin, new diabetes, medicines, or acute stress may precipitate crisis.

symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Diabetic Ketoacidosis, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.

Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.
redFlags: Shock or severe dehydration
Reduced consciousness or inability to protect airway
Severe acidosis or dangerous potassium disturbance
Pregnancy or suspected cerebral injury

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: More profound hyperosmolality and usually less prominent ketosis/acidosis; mixed presentations occur.
Exposure history and biochemical pattern differ.
May precipitate crisis or coexist; do not attribute all pain to DKA.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Blood glucose and blood ketones — Hyperglycaemia and ketonaemia
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Raised ketones with the clinical context support DKA; glucose may be less elevated in euglycaemic DKA.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Detects the metabolic emergency and tracks ketone resolution alongside acid-base results.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Venous blood gas and electrolytes — Metabolic acidosis and potassium disturbance
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced pH/bicarbonate with ketonaemia supports ketoacidosis; measured potassium may mask total-body depletion.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines severity and guides safe treatment and monitoring under the current Saudi DKA protocol.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Creatinine and fluid-balance assessment — Dehydration and kidney impairment
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Renal deterioration and fluid-balance changes help define volume loss and treatment tolerance.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports individualised fluid management and complication surveillance.

ruleOut.testName: ECG and source-directed infection tests when indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: ECG and source-directed infection tests when indicated — A cardiac/infectious precipitant or electrolyte-related arrhythmia
ruleOut.targetCondition: A cardiac/infectious precipitant or electrolyte-related arrhythmia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: ECG abnormalities or a positive source investigation directs parallel management; avoid indiscriminate cultures.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies and treats the trigger without delaying the metabolic emergency pathway.

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Determines prevention intensity and whether family assessment is appropriate.

ruleOut.targetCondition: Hypothyroidism, diabetes or organ disease contributing to dyslipidaemia
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A relevant biochemical abnormality redirects assessment to a secondary contributor.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Tests the specific suspected cause rather than assuming all abnormal lipids are primary.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Review of coronary angiography and ischaemia evidence — Coronary anatomy and clinically important ischaemia

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports Heart Team selection of revascularisation strategy and shared consent.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Echocardiography — Ventricular function and associated valve disease
ruleIn.targetCondition: Ventricular function and associated valve disease
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Systolic dysfunction or important valve pathology influences procedural risk and planning.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Defines cardiac function before the proposed intervention.

ruleOut.testName: Full blood count, creatinine and medication review
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Full blood count, creatinine and medication review — Anaemia, kidney dysfunction and bleeding/antithrombotic risk
ruleOut.targetCondition: Anaemia, kidney dysfunction and bleeding/antithrombotic risk
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Anaemia or impaired kidney function may require optimisation; document antiplatelet and anticoagulant exposure.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Plans safe contrast/procedural care and avoids preventable bleeding or medicine interruption.

This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

content.title: Maternal Sepsis in Pregnancy or Postpartum

pathophysiology.summary: Infection triggers dysregulated host response, endothelial injury, vasodilation, and organ dysfunction. Pregnancy and postpartum changes may mask early signs, and source control is as important as antimicrobial treatment. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Infection triggers dysregulated host response, endothelial injury, vasodilation, and organ dysfunction. Pregnancy and postpartum changes may mask early signs, and source control is as important as antimicrobial treatment.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Maternal Sepsis in Pregnancy or Postpartum, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.

content.title: Nausea and Vomiting in Advanced Illness

pathophysiology.summary: Nausea and vomiting arise from interacting gastrointestinal, vestibular, metabolic, intracranial, medication, and emotional inputs. Advanced illness can produce multiple simultaneous causes; symptom pattern and goals guide proportionate assessment. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Nausea and vomiting arise from interacting gastrointestinal, vestibular, metabolic, intracranial, medication, and emotional inputs. Advanced illness can produce multiple simultaneous causes
symptom pattern and goals guide proportionate assessment.

symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Nausea and Vomiting in Advanced Illness, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.
redFlags: Bilious/feculent vomiting or severe distension
GI bleeding, severe dehydration, or electrolyte concern
New severe headache or raised intracranial pressure concern
Uncontrolled symptoms or inability to take essential medicines

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Temporal relation, dose change and polypharmacy may contribute.
Bowel history and abdominal findings guide evaluation.
Symptoms and focused exam identify targeted work-up.

ruleIn.testName: Focused symptom, bowel and medication assessment
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Focused symptom, bowel and medication assessment — Drug-related, gastrointestinal or central triggers
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Timing, vomiting pattern, bowel function and recent medicine changes help identify the mechanism.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Selects symptom treatment according to the likely cause and feasible administration route.

ruleOut.testName: Glucose, electrolytes, calcium and creatinine when results change care
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Glucose, electrolytes, calcium and creatinine when results change care — A metabolic contributor or complication of vomiting
ruleOut.targetCondition: A metabolic contributor or complication of vomiting
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Hypercalcaemia, dysglycaemia, kidney impairment or electrolyte loss may explain symptoms.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Detects reversible causes and supports safe, proportionate symptom management.

ruleOut.testName: Targeted imaging if obstruction or another structural cause is suspected
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Targeted imaging if obstruction or another structural cause is suspected — A structural cause amenable to intervention
ruleOut.targetCondition: A structural cause amenable to intervention
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Imaging may demonstrate obstruction or another focal lesion relevant to the symptoms.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Use when the finding can change a goal-concordant intervention; avoid routine imaging without a decision.

Age, prior fracture, glucocorticoid exposure, low body weight, falls, and secondary disease shape risk and prevention. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Reduced bone strength reflects impaired bone mass, microarchitecture, or both, increasing fragility-fracture risk. Age, prior fracture, glucocorticoid exposure, low body weight, falls, and secondary disease shape risk and prevention.
Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Guides the haemorrhage/transfusion pathway without delaying immediate treatment.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Blood group and crossmatch — Compatible blood products
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Compatibility testing enables appropriate transfusion support.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Prepares urgently needed products through the local major-haemorrhage protocol.

ruleOut.testName: Focused obstetric examination with ultrasound when useful
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Focused obstetric examination with ultrasound when useful — Atony, trauma, retained tissue or another bleeding cause
ruleOut.targetCondition: Atony, trauma, retained tissue or another bleeding cause
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Uterine tone, genital trauma or retained tissue directs cause-specific intervention.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies the source; imaging must not delay action for clinically evident haemorrhage.

pathophysiology.summary: Preterm labour involves uterine activity with cervical remodelling before term and may arise spontaneously or from infection, placental disease, or maternal/fetal indication. Neonatal risk depends strongly on gestational age and available care. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms disease and informs management before treatment selection.

ruleOut.targetCondition: Nodal or distant spread

ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Prevents under- or over-staging and guides multidisciplinary treatment planning.

This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.

ruleIn.targetCondition: Fetal viability and immediate heart-rate concern

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Gestation-appropriate cardiotocography — A concerning fetal heart-rate pattern
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A non-reassuring pattern changes urgency; a reassuring trace does not exclude all placental or growth problems.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Evaluates short-term fetal wellbeing through the locally adopted pregnancy pathway.

ruleOut.targetCondition: Growth restriction or placental dysfunction
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Small size, reduced fluid or abnormal Doppler may explain risk despite a reassuring initial assessment.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Investigates persistent/recurrent concern or relevant risk factors and guides senior follow-up.

Insulin, secretagogues, reduced intake, renal impairment, alcohol, and acute illness can cause prolonged or recurrent episodes. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Glucose delivery falls below cerebral demand

counter-regulatory responses may be blunted by recurrent events or autonomic dysfunction. Insulin, secretagogues, reduced intake, renal impairment, alcohol, and acute illness can cause prolonged or recurrent episodes.

symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Severe Hypoglycaemia, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.

Recurrent low glucose after initial response
Persistent focal deficit after glucose correction
Suspected overdose, trauma, or inability to maintain glucose safely

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Persistent focal signs after euglycaemia need urgent neurological work-up.
Consider if events persist after correction or history supports it.
Consider when context or recovery is atypical.

ruleIn.testName: Immediate bedside glucose with repeat measurement
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Immediate bedside glucose with repeat measurement — Low glucose and response to correction
ruleIn.targetCondition: Low glucose and response to correction
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A low result supports hypoglycaemia; a repeat measurement checks recovery or recurrence.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms the reversible emergency and monitors treatment without delaying immediate care.

ruleOut.testName: Medication, intake and renal/hepatic assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Medication, intake and renal/hepatic assessment — Drug accumulation, missed intake or impaired glucose regulation
ruleOut.targetCondition: Drug accumulation, missed intake or impaired glucose regulation
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Recent insulin/sulfonylurea exposure, poor intake or organ dysfunction may explain prolonged or recurrent episodes.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies the trigger and determines monitoring needs and recurrence prevention.

ruleOut.testName: Specialist-directed critical-sample testing for unexplained recurrent episodes
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Specialist-directed critical-sample testing for unexplained recurrent episodes — Endogenous or exogenous hyperinsulinaemia and other causes
ruleOut.targetCondition: Endogenous or exogenous hyperinsulinaemia and other causes
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Selected glucose, insulin-related and exposure assays require interpretation at the time of a documented episode.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Investigates unexplained hypoglycaemia; sample collection must never delay emergency correction.

content.title: Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

pathophysiology.summary: Pregnancy increases venous stasis and coagulation tendency while reducing fibrinolysis; risk remains elevated postpartum. Thromboembolism threatens maternal oxygenation and requires coordinated diagnostic and anticoagulation planning. This topic is educational and should be interpreted alongside current local pathways and patient-specific assessment.
keyMechanisms: Pregnancy increases venous stasis and coagulation tendency while reducing fibrinolysis
risk remains elevated postpartum. Thromboembolism threatens maternal oxygenation and requires coordinated diagnostic and anticoagulation planning.

symptoms: Evaluate the characteristic symptom pattern of Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum, including onset, evolution, severity, associated symptoms, precipitating factors, complications, and relevant negative findings.
Clarify onset, progression, associated symptoms, baseline function, medicines and the patient’s own priorities.
Ask about relevant risk factors and context described in the case; document important negative findings rather than assuming their absence.
physicalSigns: Record observations and a focused examination directed to the organ system and competing diagnoses in this topic.
Assess functional change, comorbidity, hydration/perfusion where relevant, and baseline status.
Use serial reassessment when the condition or treatment can change over hours or days.
redFlags: Syncope, hypoxaemia, shock, or severe chest pain
Rapidly progressive swelling or suspected phlegmasia
Major bleeding or thrombocytopenia
Labour or planned neuraxial procedure while anticoagulated

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Usually bilateral and gradual but does not exclude DVT.
Alternative causes of chest symptoms.
Peripartum collapse is distinct and immediately critical.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Compression ultrasound for suspected DVT — Venous thrombosis
ruleIn.expectedFinding: A non-compressible vein supports DVT; persistent suspicion after a negative study requires the pregnancy-specific follow-up pathway.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides first-line objective assessment of symptomatic leg-vein thrombosis.

ruleIn.testName: Pregnancy-adapted PE assessment and specialist-selected chest imaging
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Pregnancy-adapted PE assessment and specialist-selected chest imaging — Pulmonary embolism
ruleIn.expectedFinding: The selected V/Q or CT pulmonary angiographic study is interpreted within the pregnancy diagnostic pathway.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms or excludes PE with an appropriate balance of clinical risk, radiation and contrast considerations.

ruleOut.testName: Full blood count, creatinine and bleeding assessment
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Full blood count, creatinine and bleeding assessment — Anaemia, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment or bleeding risk
ruleOut.targetCondition: Anaemia, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment or bleeding risk
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Abnormal platelets/haemoglobin or renal function may change anticoagulation and monitoring.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Establishes treatment safety without delaying urgent care for a suspected high-risk thromboembolic event.
